title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action

paper.title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Training Dynamics Action
paper.abstract:
Abstract One-step generative models construct a static generator through iterative training-time transport.
Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, although a neural generator needs to realize the requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates.
The training-time construction raises the question: once training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what to optimize: the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map? To address the question, we introduce T raining D ynamics A ction ( TDAction ), which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining a prescribed level of distributional progress.
We formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch.
The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs; under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings.
Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding an inference-time trajectory.
Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action.
On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , TDAction attains an FID below 1.1 1.1 without distillation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative modeling learns a map G θ G_{\theta} whose pushforward of a simple reference distribution matches a complex data distribution, q θ = ( G θ ) # ​ p ref ≈ p data q_{\theta}=(G_{\theta})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{ref}}\approx p_{\rm{data}} . Diffusion and flow models make the difficult transport tractable by decomposing the transport into a sequence of simpler transformations [ 36 , 18 , 39 , 27 , 28 ] . The sequence is then executed at inference, requiring repeated network evaluations for every sample. One-step generation instead seeks the same endpoint with a static map evaluated once. The challenge is to retain the flexibility of iterative transport while constructing the transport during training rather than executing the transport at inference. Figure 1 summarizes the training-time perspective by comparing the resulting distributional trajectories, target mismatch, and generator action across representative training-dynamics methods. Figure 1 : Training Dynamics Action (TDAction). Illustrative two-dimensional transport comparison. (a) Distribution trajectories during training. (b) TDAction lowers target mismatch more rapidly through progress-preserving, generator-compatible displacements. (c) At matched progress, TDAction uses the least normalized action. All methods retain one-step inference. Drifting [ 7 ] makes the training-time shift explicit. Drifting lets the generator pushforward evolve through the iterations already present in neural-network optimization, while the final trained network remains a one-step map at inference. The drifting field supplies local sample displacements from the current generated and data distributions. Training dynamics become part of the generative construction rather than only the numerical procedure used to fit a fixed objective. Sinkhorn-Drifting [ 17 ] uses two-sided Sinkhorn scaling to relate the Sinkhorn-Drifting training field to a Sinkhorn-divergence construction. The identifiability results apply under the settings stated in the cited work. W-Flow [ 16 ] separately formulates training-time updates through descent of a distributional energy. The W-Flow Sinkhorn-divergence construction gives the target field an optimal-transport interpretation before the static generator absorbs the resulting targets. Drifting, Sinkhorn-Drifting, and W-Flow share an optimal-transport viewpoint, but none is a prerequisite for the others. However, a distributional energy does not measure the difficulty of realizing a move with the finite generator currently being trained. Samples in a neural generator do not move independently: one shared parameter update needs to jointly produce the displacement of the entire batch. Two couplings that make comparable distributional progress can require different optimizer effort, or can differ in how much of the requested displacement for each coupling lies outside the generator’s local tangent space. Energy evaluates the desirability of a distributional state; action prices the motion required of the generator. The distinction is structural rather than a limitation claim about W-Flow: distribution-space steepest descent and shared-parameter realization cost need not coincide. This leads to a natural question: Among transports that make comparable progress toward the data distribution, which one incurs the lowest local realization cost for a finite generator? To answer this question, we propose T raining D ynamics A ction ( TDAction ), an action-driven principle for training-time construction of persistent one-step generators. TDAction retains distributional energy as a progress requirement and selects, among progress-preserving couplings, the one with the least local shared-parameter action to realize. For a latent batch, a coupling induces a barycentric joint displacement d π d_{\pi} . The corresponding geometry is the shared tangent mobility K θ = J θ ​ R θ − 1 ​ J θ ⊤ K_{\theta}=J_{\theta}R_{\theta}^{-1}J_{\theta}^{\top} , because a single parameter increment serves every element of the batch. The resulting Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value jointly measures optimizer effort and soft terminal mismatch, rather than assigning independent pairwise distances. One shared plan then forms detached training targets, while inference remains one evaluation of the static generator. The four methods make complementary choices about training-time transport. Drifting specifies a field, Sinkhorn-Drifting uses a balanced Sinkhorn construction, and W-Flow selects a distributional descent direction. TDAction instead selects, among moves with sufficient specified progress, the one with the lowest local shared-parameter action. TDAction does not replace the energy or field defining progress, and TDAction introduces no generative-time path objective. Our main contributions are: • An action-driven formulation of one-step generator training. We identify the optimizer-time trajectory of a persistent generator map as the relevant variational object and formulate the map’s local terminal-constrained construction as a Batch Tangent Action-to-Go problem (Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). The formulation aligns the training-time object being optimized with the static map ultimately deployed at inference. • A generator-aware Action-to-Go principle and theory. We characterize the gap between distributional transport and persistent-map construction through the same-latent trajectory and the shared tangent projection residual. Action-to-Go replaces purely geometric distance-to-go with a local parameter action. The criterion recovers quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings under isotropic mobility and gives a deterministic-assignment separation under anisotropic shared-parameter dynamics (Section 3.8 ). • A scalable realization of TDAction. Active randomized probes estimate the local mobility, and one shared Action-to-Go plan supplies detached multi-representation targets for the standard one-step training pipeline (Sections 3.5 – 3.7 ). Planning is used only during training, which keeps the resulting system a single static generator at inference. Section 4 evaluates the estimator and action criterion in controlled studies and records the available ImageNet checkpoint diagnostic.

sections.heading: One-step generation and training-time transport.
sections.text: Diffusion, score-based, flow-matching, and rectified-flow models use continuous or discretized transport constructions [ 36 , 18 , 39 , 27 , 28 ] . Direct generators and distillation methods seek to reduce the resulting sampling cost [ 15 , 1 , 34 , 37 ] . Drifting, Sinkhorn-Drifting, and W-Flow accumulate training-time transport in a generator while retaining one-step inference [ 7 , 17 , 16 ] . Sinkhorn-Drifting relates the drifting field to Sinkhorn-divergence flow through full two-sided balancing, whereas W-Flow starts from a distributional energy and follows the corresponding Wasserstein gradient flow. TDAction uses the same deployment setting, but evaluates a candidate coupling through the optimizer-time effort required to realize the coupling’s joint batch displacement.

sections.heading: Distributional geometry and action.
sections.text: Optimal transport and Sinkhorn divergences provide discrepancies and geometries for generative modeling [ 12 , 9 , 33 ] . The Benamou–Brenier formulation characterizes kinetic action for a probability path [ 2 ] , and Wasserstein gradient flow specifies local steepest descent of a functional on measures [ 21 ] . Parameterized Wasserstein gradient flow studies the effect of restricting such geometry to a model family [ 20 ] . Action Matching also studies variational actions for probability-path learning [ 31 ] . The distinction between a drift field and a state-energy gradient is also formalized for non-conservative drifting fields [ 11 ] . TDAction instead uses the optimizer-time tangent geometry of a persistent generator and does not optimize a generative-time density path.

sections.heading: Model-aware and minibatch couplings.
sections.text: Model-Aligned Coupling (MAC) observes that geometric OT pairs can disagree with directions that a learned flow-matching model predicts reliably, and selects pairs using model error [ 26 ] . TDAction differs by pricing a joint endpoint displacement with a shared-parameter control value, rather than scoring pairs with a generative-time prediction error. Repeated minibatch OT also induces an expected batch plan whose cost and coupling can differ from population OT [ 3 ] . Batch size, coupling persistence, and held-out action prediction are method-level quantities rather than implementation details.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Training Dynamics Action (TDAction), an action-driven principle for constructing persistent one-step generators during training. Building on the training-time transport perspectives of Drifting and W-Flow, TDAction asks which sufficiently progressive transport a finite shared-parameter generator learns. The Batch Tangent Action-to-Go formulation incorporates generator realizability directly into target selection: the local control value captures optimizer effort and soft terminal mismatch, while the progress constraint prevents a low action from being obtained by under-moving the distribution. The formulation recovers quadratic Euclidean assignment in the isotropic deterministic case, distinguishes distribution-optimal from generator-action-optimal transport under anisotropic shared-parameter dynamics, and confines all action-based planning to training; inference remains a single evaluation of a static generator. Empirically, TDAction attains FID below 1.1 1.1 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 with one-step generation, improving on the preceding Drifting and W-Flow training-time transport baselines while preserving one-NFE deployment. The controlled studies and the ImageNet result support the central hypothesis that reducing the realization cost of a useful transport helps a finite generator turn distributional progress into a high-quality one-step map. The present implementation still relies on a local tangent approximation, a chosen representation and optimizer metric, and finite-sample mobility estimates; longer-horizon or curvature-aware action values, more efficient estimation, and richer conditional or multimodal generators remain open directions for future work.

sections.heading: Generator, frozen representations, and conditioning.
sections.text: A TDAction ImageNet executor leaves the DiT forward map unchanged. The executor maps latent noise, an ImageNet class, and a code-level guidance condition to an SD-VAE latent sample; the VAE decoder is required only for RGB visualization and final evaluation. The planning representation ψ \psi and the regression representations { ϕ ℓ } ℓ = 1 L \{\phi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} are frozen latent-MAE features. Gradients through the feature activations with respect to the generator output are retained, but the feature-encoder parameters are not updated. TDAction changes target construction rather than the generator architecture, the frozen feature catalog, or the inference topology.

sections.heading: Canonical supports and class-conditioned global plans.
sections.text: At a support refresh, the implementation fixes source latents Z Z , real examples X X , generated canonical features U U , and real canonical features Y Y . The batch map and the corresponding Jacobian are given by Eq. 7 . For class-conditional generation, generated and real elements are matched only within the same conditioning class; the class restriction keeps the global plan block structured and prevents transport across classes. The complete planner state is 𝒮 k = ( Z k , X k , U k , Y k , K ^ k , π k − 1 ) . \mathcal{S}_{k}=(Z_{k},X_{k},U_{k},Y_{k},\widehat{K}_{k},\pi_{k-1}). The mobility sketch and coupling are valid only on the canonical support. A new support requires a new sketch before an anisotropic plan is formed; a sketch estimated on one batch is not applied to a different batch.

sections.heading: Active mobility estimation.
sections.text: The frozen control metric R θ ≻ 0 R_{\theta}\succ 0 defines the shared-parameter mobility in Eq. 8 . At a refresh, independent randomized parameter probes ξ s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \xi_{s}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) yield response vectors r s = J θ R θ − 1 / 2 ξ s , K ^ θ = 1 M ∑ s = 1 M r s r s ⊤ . r_{s}=J_{\theta}R_{\theta}^{-1/2}\xi_{s},\qquad\widehat{K}_{\theta}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{s=1}^{M}r_{s}r_{s}^{\top}. The primary probe bank constructs the plan, while an independent shadow bank is reserved for held-out action and agreement diagnostics. Observed AdamW updates cannot replace the probes because AdamW responses depend jointly on the current loss, data batch, and optimizer state. The control metric, both probe counts, the support-refresh cadence, the retained rank, and the sketch floor belong in Table 8 .

The amortized probe cost is controlled by the refresh interval. The executor computes the Euclidean entropic anchor on the same canonical supports and tests the anchor’s first-order progress. When the anchor progress is positive, the executor solves Eq. 15 with a fixed number of KL mirror steps. Each multiplicative step is followed by a Bregman projection restoring the coupling marginals by Sinkhorn scaling and enforcing the linear progress constraint through a scalar dual update. Persistence is used only for aligned replay supports. If the Euclidean anchor has nonpositive progress, the executor returns the Euclidean anchor and does not select a near-identity low-action plan.

sections.heading: Shared detached targets and support persistence.
sections.text: One canonical coupling supplies the latent-to-endpoint identity for every frozen regression representation. The row-normalized plan maps the real features to barycentric endpoints as specified in Eq. 18 , and the detached feature targets and ordinary regression loss are given in Eqs. 19 and 20 . Gradients flow through the generator and feature activations, but never through the coupling solver, mobility sketch, or target increments. During an aligned support window, the support, sketch, and previous coupling can be reused. At the next refresh, the implementation recomputes the primary and shadow probes and resets persistence unless an explicit replay correspondence is available.

sections.heading: Distributed execution and training iteration.
sections.text: Multi-GPU execution has one logical canonical plan. Canonical features and probe responses may be computed locally, but the responses are gathered in the same canonical order before solving the coupling. After the solve, each worker receives only the rows required to form local barycentric targets and performs the usual distributed gradient reduction. Feature extraction, JVPs, barycentric feature mapping, regression losses, and backward accumulation may be streamed or partitioned for memory. Independently planning per GPU or per microbatch would omit cross-particle mobility blocks and would define a different algorithm. A complete TDAction iteration proceeds as follows: 1. Sample class labels, the training guidance condition, latent noise, and matching real examples. 2. At a refresh step, construct ( U , Y ) (U,Y) and update the independent primary and shadow mobility estimates. 3. Form the Euclidean entropic anchor, evaluate the anchor progress, and solve the constrained Batch-ATG problem when the anchor is admissible. 4. Reuse the selected coupling to construct detached barycentric targets at all frozen regression levels. 5. Evaluate the ordinary regression loss, apply one optimizer update, update the EMA generator, and write the audit record.

sections.heading: Diagnostics, guidance, evaluation, and cost.
sections.text: The planned action is a tangent-model quantity, whereas the optimizer produces an executed parameter increment δ exec \delta_{\mathrm{exec}} . A diagnostic run records the nonnegative local execution gap Δ exec ​ ( π ) = 1 2 ​ δ exec ⊤ ​ R θ ​ δ exec + 1 2 ​ ρ ​ ‖ J θ ​ δ exec − d π ‖ 2 2 − V ρ ​ ( π ) . \Delta_{\mathrm{exec}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{2}\delta_{\mathrm{exec}}^{\top}R_{\theta}\delta_{\mathrm{exec}}+\frac{1}{2\rho}\left\|J_{\theta}\delta_{\mathrm{exec}}-d_{\pi}\right\|_{2}^{2}-V_{\rho}(\pi). The audit record also includes primary and shadow action, planned and post-update progress, projection and marginal residuals, target-realization cosine, plan churn, solver feasibility, step time, and allocated and reserved memory. CFG is an outer conditioning and inference control, not a retrospective criterion for choosing a training coupling. A completed comparison selects the code scale on disjoint generated samples, evaluates the frozen EMA checkpoint on a held-out 50K class-balanced sample set, and records the checkpoint and configuration hashes, sampling seeds, real-statistics file, sample count, and evaluator version. The active probes, low-rank solve, and communication buffers are training-time components only. At inference, the EMA generator retains the one-step deployment topology of the reference generators.

sections.heading: A.16 Status of the available evidence
sections.text: The completed low-dimensional studies in the appendix document the action question and include adverse controls. The studies do not validate the active Batch-ATG executor. The corresponding Fréchet quantities are two-dimensional Gaussian-moment proxies, not ImageNet FID. The fixed-checkpoint ImageNet record is included below as a diagnostic of the passive precursor, not as a formal comparative result.

sections.heading: Matched outer-loop protocol.
sections.text: A completed TDAction comparison holds the DiT backbone, latent representation, class-conditioning protocol, optimizer schedule, EMA rule, effective global batch, data order, and evaluation statistic file fixed. TDAction changes only the target construction: the method replaces an Euclidean or energy-derived coupling with the progress-constrained Batch Tangent Action-to-Go problem in Eq. 15 . We do not present inherited baseline settings as completed TDAction hyperparameters.

sections.heading: Canonical batch and distributed execution.
sections.text: Each mobility sketch is tied to the source latents and real examples that define the global canonical batch ( U , Y ) (U,Y) through the frozen map ψ \psi in Eq. 7 . The plan may reuse the canonical support within a refresh window, but a newly sampled support requires a new sketch; applying a sketch to a different batch is not part of the method. Feature extraction may be partitioned across devices or microbatches, but the planning supports are gathered before forming the coupling. The resulting π k ⋆ \pi_{k}^{\star} is the sole latent-to-endpoint identity for all feature levels in Eq. 18 ; each worker receives only the rows required for local backward processing. Independent per-device couplings are not equivalent to TDAction because independent couplings remove the cross-particle blocks of K θ K_{\theta} and change the optimization problem. Gradient accumulation is a memory implementation of one global plan, rather than a sequence of independently planned microbatches.

sections.heading: Mobility probes and plan optimization.
sections.text: The geometry refresh uses primary random probes to construct the low-rank approximation K ^ θ ≈ B ​ B ⊤ + σ 2 ​ I \widehat{K}_{\theta}\approx BB^{\top}+\sigma^{2}I and conditionally independent shadow probes to assess the selected plan. The control metric R θ R_{\theta} is specified as a positive, frozen planning metric at the refresh; observed AdamW updates cannot replace the probes because the updates confound the current loss, data batch, and optimizer state. Between aligned support refreshes, the sketch is held fixed and the coupling solver uses the prescribed terminal tolerance ρ \rho , entropy ε \varepsilon , persistence weight λ p \lambda_{\mathrm{p}} , progress fraction γ \gamma , and a fixed mirror-step budget. The persistence term is enabled only when replay supports are aligned. If the Euclidean anchor has nonpositive progress, the implementation returns the Euclidean anchor, as required by Eq. 15 , instead of selecting a low-action near-identity plan.

sections.heading: Targets, memory, and audit trail.
sections.text: The plan, mobility sketch, and barycentric targets are detached before the ordinary multi-representation regression loss in Eq. 20 . Low-rank Woodbury products are used for the action value; forming the dense global n ​ d × n ​ d nd\times nd mobility is neither required nor representative of the intended scalable implementation. A completed run logs the primary and shadow split, refresh cadence, support reuse, sketch rank and ridge, planned progress ratio, post-update energy change, projection residual, target-realization cosine, plan churn, solver marginal error, progress violation, and held-out shadow action ratio, in addition to step time and allocated and reserved memory. The audit records distinguish a lower regularized surrogate value from an improvement in realized action at matched progress.

sections.heading: Guidance and evaluation separation.
sections.text: Classifier-free guidance is an inference control and is not used to choose a training coupling retrospectively. For the available frozen 56K-step precursor, the code scale s = 1.25 s=1.25 was selected on the disjoint 10K-sample seed-0 sweep and evaluated once with 50K class-balanced samples at seed 2027. The same disjoint selection rule, fixed generated-sample count, and held-out statistic file are required for a completed matched TDAction experiment. The precursor did not record active primary and shadow probes or the required held-out action audit; the precursor remains excluded from claims about the Batch-ATG implementation.

Affiliation: Department of Artificial Intelligence, Westlake University Email: linghaibin@westlake.edu.cn Abstract One-step generative models construct a static generator through iterative training-time transport. Existing transport objectives primarily assess distributional motion, although a neural generator needs to realize the requested sample displacements jointly through shared parameter updates. The training-time construction raises the question: once training becomes the iterative process that constructs the final one-step map, what to optimize: the next distributional move, or the route by which the finite generator learns the final map? To address the question, we introduce T raining D ynamics A ction ( TDAction ), which selects transport targets according to local shared-parameter realization cost while retaining a prescribed level of distributional progress. We formulate the cost as a soft-terminal control problem and derive a closed-form Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value that accounts for parameter effort and terminal mismatch. The criterion captures cross-sample interactions omitted by independent pairwise costs; under isotropic mobility, the criterion agrees with quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings. Randomized tangent probes provide a low-rank implementation that constructs shared detached targets without adding an inference-time trajectory. Controlled studies examine the relationship between generator geometry, transport selection, and realized local action. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256	imes 256 , TDAction attains an FID below 1.1 1.1 without distillation. 1 Introduction Generative modeling learns a map G θ G_{	heta} whose pushforward of a simple reference distribution matches a complex data distribution, q θ = ( G θ ) # ​ p ref ≈ p data q_{	heta}=(G_{	heta})_{\#}p_{\mathrm{ref}}\approx p_{m{data}} . Diffusion and flow models make the difficult transport tractable by decomposing the transport into a sequence of simpler transformations [ 36 , 18 , 39 , 27 , 28 ] . The sequence is then executed at inference, requiring repeated network evaluations for every sample. One-step generation instead seeks the same endpoint with a static map evaluated once. The challenge is to retain the flexibility of iterative transport while constructing the transport during training rather than executing the transport at inference. Figure 1 summarizes the training-time perspective by comparing the resulting distributional trajectories, target mismatch, and generator action across representative training-dynamics methods. Figure 1 : Training Dynamics Action (TDAction). Illustrative two-dimensional transport comparison. (a) Distribution trajectories during training. (b) TDAction lowers target mismatch more rapidly through progress-preserving, generator-compatible displacements. (c) At matched progress, TDAction uses the least normalized action. All methods retain one-step inference. Drifting [ 7 ] makes the training-time shift explicit. Drifting lets the generator pushforward evolve through the iterations already present in neural-network optimization, while the final trained network remains a one-step map at inference. The drifting field supplies local sample displacements from the current generated and data distributions. Training dynamics become part of the generative construction rather than only the numerical procedure used to fit a fixed objective. Sinkhorn-Drifting [ 17 ] uses two-sided Sinkhorn scaling to relate the Sinkhorn-Drifting training field to a Sinkhorn-divergence construction. The identifiability results apply under the settings stated in the cited work. W-Flow [ 16 ] separately formulates training-time updates through descent of a distributional energy. The W-Flow Sinkhorn-divergence construction gives the target field an optimal-transport interpretation before the static generator absorbs the resulting targets. Drifting, Sinkhorn-Drifting, and W-Flow share an optimal-transport viewpoint, but none is a prerequisite for the others. However, a distributional energy does not measure the difficulty of realizing a move with the finite generator currently being trained. Samples in a neural generator do not move independently: one shared parameter update needs to jointly produce the displacement of the entire batch. Two couplings that make comparable distributional progress can require different optimizer effort, or can differ in how much of the requested displacement for each coupling lies outside the generator’s local tangent space. Energy evaluates the desirability of a distributional state; action prices the motion required of the generator. The distinction is structural rather than a limitation claim about W-Flow: distribution-space steepest descent and shared-parameter realization cost need not coincide. This leads to a natural question: Among transports that make comparable progress toward the data distribution, which one incurs the lowest local realization cost for a finite generator? To answer this question, we propose T raining D ynamics A ction ( TDAction ), an action-driven principle for training-time construction of persistent one-step generators. TDAction retains distributional energy as a progress requirement and selects, among progress-preserving couplings, the one with the least local shared-parameter action to realize. For a latent batch, a coupling induces a barycentric joint displacement d π d_{\pi} . The corresponding geometry is the shared tangent mobility K θ = J θ ​ R θ − 1 ​ J θ ⊤ K_{	heta}=J_{	heta}R_{	heta}^{-1}J_{	heta}^{	op} , because a single parameter increment serves every element of the batch. The resulting Batch Tangent Action-to-Go value jointly measures optimizer effort and soft terminal mismatch, rather than assigning independent pairwise distances. One shared plan then forms detached training targets, while inference remains one evaluation of the static generator. The four methods make complementary choices about training-time transport. Drifting specifies a field, Sinkhorn-Drifting uses a balanced Sinkhorn construction, and W-Flow selects a distributional descent direction. TDAction instead selects, among moves with sufficient specified progress, the one with the lowest local shared-parameter action. TDAction does not replace the energy or field defining progress, and TDAction introduces no generative-time path objective. Our main contributions are: • An action-driven formulation of one-step generator training. We identify the optimizer-time trajectory of a persistent generator map as the relevant variational object and formulate the map’s local terminal-constrained construction as a Batch Tangent Action-to-Go problem (Sections 3.3 and 3.4 ). The formulation aligns the training-time object being optimized with the static map ultimately deployed at inference. • A generator-aware Action-to-Go principle and theory. We characterize the gap between distributional transport and persistent-map construction through the same-latent trajectory and the shared tangent projection residual. Action-to-Go replaces purely geometric distance-to-go with a local parameter action. The criterion recovers quadratic Euclidean assignment for deterministic balanced couplings under isotropic mobility and gives a deterministic-assignment separation under anisotropic shared-parameter dynamics (Section 3.8 ). • A scalable realization of TDAction. Active randomized probes estimate the local mobility, and one shared Action-to-Go plan supplies detached multi-representation targets for the standard one-step training pipeline (Sections 3.5 – 3.7 ). Planning is used only during training, which keeps the resulting system a single static generator at inference. Section 4 evaluates the estimator and action criterion in controlled studies and records the available ImageNet checkpoint diagnostic. 2 Related Work One-step generation and training-time transport. Diffusion, score-based, flow-matching, and rectified-flow models use continuous or discretized transport constructions [ 36 , 18 , 39 , 27 , 28 ] . Direct generators and distillation methods seek to reduce the resulting sampling cost [ 15 , 1 , 34 , 37 ] . Drifting, Sinkhorn-Drifting, and W-Flow accumulate training-time transport in a generator while retaining one-step inference [ 7 , 17 , 16 ] . Sinkhorn-Drifting relates the drifting field to Sinkhorn-divergence flow through full two-sided balancing, whereas W-Flow starts from a distributional energy and follows the corresponding Wasserstein gradient flow. TDAction uses the same deployment setting, but evaluates a candidate coupling through the optimizer-time effort required to realize the coupling’s joint batch displacement. Distributional geometry and action. Optimal transport and Sinkhorn divergences provide discrepancies and geometries for generative modeling [ 12 , 9 , 33 ] . The Benamou–Brenier formulation characterizes kinetic action for a probability path [ 2 ] , and Wasserstein gradient flow specifies local steepest descent of a functional on measures [ 21 ] . Parameterized Wasserstein gradient flow studies the effect of restricting such geometry to a model family [ 20 ] . Action Matching also studies variational actions for probability-path learning [ 31 ] . The distinction between a drift field and a state-energy gradient is also formalized for non-conservative drifting fields [ 11 ] . TDAction instead uses the optimizer-time tangent geometry of a persistent generator and does not optimize a generative-time density path. Model-aware and minibatch couplings. Model-Aligned Coupling (MAC) observes that geometric OT pairs can disagree with directions that a learned flow-matching model predicts reliably, and selects pairs using model error [ 26 ] . TDAction differs by pricing a joint endpoint displacement with a shared-parameter control value, rather than scoring pairs with a generative-time prediction error. Repeated minibatch OT also induces an expected batch plan whose cost and coupling can differ from population OT [ 3 ] .
